rules.title: Hard-coded credential or API key assigned in source
rules.why: A credential committed to source is a credential leaked to everyone with repo access, plus every copy of the repo and every CI log.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Very high FP rate. Exclude: placeholder values (CHANGEME, xxx, your-key-here, <secret>), test fixtures, config keys with empty strings, variable NAMES without values, and templated values (${VAR}, {{var}}, %ENV%). Confirm the value looks like a real secret before reporting.

rules.title: Private key material embedded in the repository
rules.why: An embedded private key compromises every identity, signature or channel it protects.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Test fixtures still count as findings if the key is also used outside tests. A dedicated throwaway test key is Low, not Critical - but verify it is not referenced by production config.

rules.title: Cloud provider access key literal
rules.why: Provider-format keys are harvested by automated scanners within minutes of being pushed.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Check whether the value is obviously fake/redacted. If real-looking, this is Critical and the key must be treated as already compromised - rotation is the remediation, not deletion from source.

rules.title: Connection string with inline password
rules.why: Database credentials in config or source are the shortest path from repo access to data exfiltration.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Exclude templated placeholders and integrated-security connection strings.

rules.title: Broken or deprecated hash algorithm
rules.why: MD5 and SHA-1 are collision-broken. For passwords they are catastrophic; for signatures they are forgeable.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Severity depends entirely on use. Password hashing or signature verification: High/Critical. Non-security checksums (cache keys, ETags, file dedupe): Info, and say so explicitly rather than flagging noise.

rules.title: Broken or weak symmetric cipher
rules.why: DES/3DES/RC4 are broken. ECB mode leaks plaintext structure regardless of the cipher.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Check it is used for confidentiality, not interop with a legacy system that mandates it. If mandated, the finding stands but the remediation becomes compensating controls.

rules.title: Insecure randomness used in a security context
rules.why: Non-cryptographic PRNGs are predictable. Tokens, session ids, password-reset codes and nonces built from them are guessable.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Only a finding when the output is used as a token, id, salt, nonce, key or password. UI jitter, shuffling display data, or test data generation is not a finding.

rules.title: TLS certificate validation disabled
rules.why: Disabling certificate validation turns TLS into unauthenticated encryption - a machine-in-the-middle reads and rewrites everything.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Local development and test code is lower severity, but confirm the switch cannot be reached in production (environment-gated, not just conventionally named).

rules.title: Cleartext HTTP endpoint for an application or API call
rules.why: Credentials, tokens and PII sent over cleartext HTTP are readable by anyone on the path.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Rust regex has no lookahead, so this pattern is deliberately broad. Filter during triage: localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, *.local, example.com, XML namespaces (xmlns), XSD/DTD schema URLs and W3C references. XML namespace URIs are identifiers, not network calls, and are never a finding.

rules.title: SQL statement assembled by string concatenation or interpolation
rules.why: Concatenated SQL is the canonical injection vector: full read, write and often OS-level access to the database host.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Confirm the interpolated value is not a compile-time constant, an enum, or a validated identifier from a fixed allow-list. Also confirm the string is actually executed rather than logged or shown as documentation. Deliberately does NOT match bare {placeholder} braces: C# $"..." passed to FromSqlInterpolated and Python f-strings passed to execute(sql, params) are parameterized and safe, and the language packs (DN-INJ-01, PY-INJ-01) cover the unsafe forms with the context needed to tell them apart.

rules.title: OS command executed with a constructed argument string
rules.why: If any part of the command line comes from untrusted input, the attacker runs code as the application user.
rules.falsePositiveHints: A fully literal command with no interpolation and shell=False is not a finding. shell=True (or a single string passed to a shell) with ANY variable content is a finding.

rules.title: Dynamic code evaluation
rules.why: Evaluating a string that any untrusted input can influence is remote code execution.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Python's exec in build tooling, or eval over a hard-coded literal, is Info. Distinguish JS `exec` on a regex (RegExp.prototype.exec / .exec(str)) - that is NOT code evaluation and is a common false positive.

rules.title: Unsafe deserialization of untrusted data
rules.why: Deserializing attacker-controlled bytes into live objects yields remote code execution in every language listed here.
rules.falsePositiveHints: yaml.safe_load is fine. Deserializing data the application itself just produced and stored in a trusted location is lower severity - but confirm the store is genuinely not attacker-writable.

rules.title: File path built from a variable without normalization
rules.why: Path traversal lets an attacker read or overwrite files outside the intended directory - config, keys, source, or the application binary.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Not a finding when the variable is a fixed server-side constant or an id already validated against an allow-list. Look for a canonicalization + prefix check; if it exists, the finding is closed.

rules.title: Potentially sensitive value written to a log
rules.why: Secrets and PII in logs spread to log aggregators, backups and support tickets, far outside the application trust boundary.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Logging the literal string "password required" or a field NAME is not a finding. Logging the VALUE is. Read the statement.

rules.title: Exception detail returned to the caller
rules.why: Stack traces disclose framework versions, file paths, SQL fragments and internal structure that shorten an attacker's reconnaissance.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Server-side logging of a stack trace is correct practice, not a finding. Only returning it to the client counts.

rules.title: Outbound HTTP request to a URL built from input
rules.why: SSRF reaches internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) and admin interfaces from inside the network perimeter.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Not a finding if the host is fixed and only the path/query is variable, or the URL is validated against a host allow-list. Confirm which part is attacker-controlled.

rules.title: XML parser configured without external-entity protection
rules.why: A parser that resolves external entities can be made to read local files or make outbound requests on the attacker's behalf.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Modern defaults are often safe (.NET 4.5.2+, Python defusedxml, recent JDKs). This is a PROMPT to check the configuration nearby, not an automatic finding. Confirm whether disallow-doctype-decl / external-general-entities is set.

rules.title: Authorization decision made against a client-supplied role or id
rules.why: Any authorization input the client controls can be forged. This is the mechanism behind most IDOR and privilege-escalation bugs.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Reading an id from the request is normal; the finding is whether an OWNERSHIP or ROLE check follows before the record is returned or mutated. Read the handler to the end before deciding.

rules.title: Developer note flagging an unresolved security concern
rules.why: Developers usually know where the weak spots are. These comments are a high-yield map of them.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Not a vulnerability in itself. Use each hit as a pointer for manual review; report only the ones whose underlying issue you confirm.
